text: A bug is in production, and an AI has written the fix. The tests pass. But the tests an AI writes only prove what it already thought of. So, should it merge?
FireDrill is an adversarial hotfix courtroom, inside a Switch chat room. One agent writes the fix. Another agent attacks it. A referee runs real tests. And a named human signs last.

There are four roles. The fixer, a Claude agent, writes the patch. The breaker, a Codex agent, writes hostile tests to break it. The gate is the referee. It runs every test in a fresh workspace, and it holds the only key to the main branch. And a named human approves, but only after the patch has survived an attack.

Switch is what makes this work. It puts agents and people in one chat room. The gate is a custom Switch agent, connected over a web socket. It reads the commands typed in the room, writes its decisions into documents that only it can edit, and checks sign-off against the Switch participant identity, not against typed words.
That gives us one simple rule. No attack, no sign-off. A patch that only passes its own repro test is green on repro only, and a human cannot approve it yet.

Here is a real run, on a real Switch server, shown in Mattermost. A patch is submitted. The gate answers in the thread, and updates its docket and verdict documents. Every ruling lands back in the room.

The dashboard tells the same story. A landing page explains the idea, and then you pick a case. A double charge caused by a race. A rate limit that lets too much through. Or a pagination bug that repeats items.

Let's watch the idempotency race. The console at the bottom prints the real room log. First, a naive patch is submitted. The gate runs the repro test, and it passes. Green, but only on the repro. Then the breaker attacks. One hostile test finds the race, and the gate marks the patch red. A real, root cause fix is submitted, and this time it survives the attack. Now, and only now, a human can approve. The gate checks who they are, and merges with its own key.

The console is a real prompt. Press enter for the next step, or type run to play on its own. Step back, jump to any page, check the status, or switch to another case. It only replays recorded frames. It never sends anything to the gate.
It works on a phone too, and it passes automated accessibility and contrast checks.

So what is real, and what is scripted? The gate, the verifier and the merge are real. We ran all three incidents against Switch zero point thirty one. Every verdict comes from real pytest runs, and the merge goes through a guarded git hook that only accepts the gate's key. What is scripted is the cast. One person posted the commands, so no Claude or Codex session took part in this recording, and we say so everywhere.
FireDrill, built for the Flip the Switch hackathon. A fix has to survive an attack before a human signs. Thanks for watching.
